notes: Both agree that ISR23 is located at the catalytic center of the ribosome and includes residues critical for peptide bond synthesis. High overlap (6/7 shared claims including C52-C56, C69). Peer review explicitly affirms the catalytic center location.

LLM finds TLR13 knockout data for multiple cytokines (C65-C68) SUPPORTED, but peer reviewers mark UNCERTAIN and explicitly request additional mRNA induction data for TNF-α, IL-6, and type I IFNs beyond IL-1β to demonstrate broader response.

Both agree that TLR cooperation claims (C95, C96) are UNCERTAIN. LLM notes these require further investigation; peer reviewers explicitly ask 'Is there any possibility that TLR13 signals in conjunction with other TLRs?' indicating this remains an open question.

Both support the pathway characterization (MyD88/Unc93b1 dependence, C31-C35, C100). Peer reviewers accept these methodological claims without question as part of their broader acceptance of the experimental approach.

Both support TLR13 knockout data for IL-1β (C29, C62, C64). Peer reviewers accept these findings without critique; their request for additional cytokines is to broaden scope, not due to doubt about IL-1β data.
Both support TLR13 identification through knockdown and rescue experiments (C37, C38). Peer reviewers accept the experimental approach without concern as part of their overall positive assessment.
Both support that 23S rRNA (not 16S) is the active ligand (C39-C43). Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of their affirmation that TLR13 recognizes specific 23S RNA sequences.
Both support the sequence specificity findings from point mutagenesis (C46-C51). Peer reviewers accept the experimental data demonstrating exquisite sequence specificity without raising concerns.

Both support identification of minimal 13-nucleotide sequence (C3, C72). Peer reviewers explicitly affirm TLR13 recognizes 'specific, conserved sequences' and accept the systematic deletion analysis approach.

Both support the core sequence-specific recognition mechanism (C4, C6, C30). Peer reviewers state this 'provides a new view of innate receptor recognition' and deem manuscript acceptable for publication.
Both support TLR13 as the receptor for bacterial RNA (C2). Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding without critique.
Both support sequence conservation claims (C57). Peer reviewers accept the conservation across bacterial species as part of their affirmation of the biological significance.
Both support the minimal sequence findings (C72). Peer reviewers acknowledge the concurrent Oldenburg publication and request discussion but do not challenge validity, indicating acceptance.
Both support the systematic deletion analysis identifying domain V (C44, C45). Peer reviewers accept the methodological approach without concern.
Both support TLR13 as essential for response to bacterial 23S rRNA (C5). Peer reviewers affirm this as the core finding of the manuscript.
LLM evaluates H. marismortui variant experiment (C58, C59) as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers do not separately address these specific experimental claims, though they accept overall conservation findings.
LLM marks evolutionary implications and autoimmune speculation (C60, C81-C88, C93) as UNCERTAIN. Peer reviewers do not address these speculative claims in their evaluation.
LLM marks claims about RNA trafficking mechanisms (C97-C99) as UNCERTAIN. Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these mechanistic speculations beyond their TLR cooperation question.
LLM marks adjuvant application claims (C101, C102) as UNCERTAIN/speculative. Peer reviewers do not address these translational speculation claims.
Peer reviewers address concurrent Oldenburg publication (C71, C73) and request discussion of similarity/novelty. LLM does not separately evaluate these contextual claims about independent validation.
